svg.aria-label: The real WireGuard handshake between the lab's Python peer and the Pi's kernel: a 148-byte initiation, a 92-byte response, then transport data

g.text: temporary key · 🔒 permanent key · 🔒 time · mac1
who is this? only a known key gets an answer

ol.li: Bob’s side sends one message: a fresh temporary public key in the clear, then its permanent public key and the time, sealed with keys from X25519 exchanges it could do already, because it knows the Pi’s public key in advance.

The Pi checks the cheap mac1 first, then opens the sealed parts. If the permanent key isn’t on its list of peers, or the timestamp is older than one it has seen (a replayed message), it says nothing at all. A port scan can’t even tell that WireGuard is there.

Its answer carries its own temporary key, and a sealed empty box: proof that it could derive the same keys, so it really holds the Pi’s private key. Both sides now mix four X25519 results into two keys, one for each direction, and throw the temporary private keys away: forward secrecy, as in TLS 1.3.
Data follows at once: whole IP packets, sealed, numbered with a counter that doubles as the nonce. Every two minutes the handshake is done again, so keys never live long.

figure.figcaption: A WireGuard handshake, with the real sizes from wg_peer.py ping talking to the Pi’s kernel.
